name: mute-idiom
intent: Absorb the failure of one specific, provably ignorable call at its call site - naming the ignored failure narrowly and writing down why it is inconsequential - so work continues without the error plumbing a failure that changes nothing would otherwise demand.
problem: A single known call can fail and its failure has been shown to be inconsequential (closing a read-only descriptor, deleting a temp file that may already be gone, releasing a lock the cleanup path no longer needs, a rejected best-effort telemetry flush), yet the failure either propagates and aborts work that had already succeeded, or is swallowed by a blanket catch that also hides failures nobody has reasoned about.
context: Error-contract decisions at a single call site in code that must continue: cleanup and release paths, best-effort notifications and cache maintenance, idempotent lifecycle operations where 'already done' is reported as an error, and compatibility shims around libraries that signal expected conditions as exceptions. It applies wherever the language has exceptions, error returns or a Result type, and only where the ignorability argument can be written down and later re-checked.
benefits: The main path stays legible: no error plumbing, no early return and no 'what if this fails' indentation around a call whose failure is already known to be harmless.
The ignore becomes explicit and reviewable: a named failure type plus a written justification converts a hidden swallow into a greppable, discussable decision.
Blanket catches stay out: because one narrow failure is muted deliberately, every other failure still reaches the caller unchanged.
Cleanup and best-effort paths can finish the work they were invoked for even when a subordinate step reports a failure that does not alter the outcome.
Idempotent operations read as idempotent: 'already absent / already released / already applied' stops being an error condition with a code path of its own.

Third-party boundaries shrink: an API that reports expected conditions (not-found, already-exists, interrupted, client hung up) as exceptions can be tolerated at one call site instead of at every caller.
tradeoffs: Silent failure is indistinguishable from success downstream: once the mute is in place, a genuine worsening of that call - data loss that only surfaces as EIO on close, a permission change, a new failure mode added by a library upgrade - produces no signal anywhere.

The justification is prose, not a check: 'provably ignorable' lives in a comment or commit message, and a refactor of the callee invalidates it without a compiler, test, linter or type error noticing.

The mute invites widening under pressure: one named exception type becomes the whole exception hierarchy, and the end state is the jOOQ parody - a helper that swallows Throwable around an entire method body.
Coverage and diagnostics degrade together: the ignored path is normally untested, and the post-mortem loses the one stack trace that would have explained the incident.

It carries permanent suppression bookkeeping: static analysis (Go's errcheck and staticcheck, Rust's must-use lints, C#'s analyzers, SonarSource rules about empty catch blocks) flags every mute, so each site needs an inline suppression and a justification to keep the build clean.

Cleanup paths are where the pattern is most tempting and most dangerous: a failed flush or close that discards buffered writes is invisible by construction, which is exactly how the POSIX EIO-on-close class of data loss is found late.

participants.responsibility: Holds the single invocation whose failure is tolerated, wrapped in the narrowest suppression construct the language offers (one exception type, one explicit discard, one suppression helper).
The specific, enumerated failure value the call can produce; its consequences have been inspected and shown not to change the outcome of the surrounding operation.
The comment, test or documented contract next to the mute that states why this failure is inconsequential and keeps the ignore from decaying into a blanket catch.
The route taken by every failure that is not the ignored one - rethrow, return, error channel, fail-closed - so the mute cannot absorb anything that was not analysed.

use_cases: Releasing resources in cleanup or destructor paths: closing an already-closed read-only handle, unmapping a best-effort file, releasing a lock the shutdown path no longer needs.
Best-effort filesystem and cache maintenance: unlinking a stale temp file that may already be gone, invalidating a cache key another thread removed first, trimming an eviction that lost the race.

Idempotent lifecycle operations: stopping a service that is not running, deleting an object that does not exist, unmounting an already unmounted resource - the caller asked for the end state, not for the transition.
Compatibility shims around libraries that report expected conditions as exceptions (not-found, already-exists, interrupted, broken pipe when the peer hung up first).
Fire-and-forget telemetry, metrics and notification flushes where losing one data point is acceptable and failing the request is not.
Interrupt or shutdown paths where the interrupt status is restored afterwards and the subordinate failure is documented as expected during teardown.

Python's standard-library `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)` around `os.remove` is a concrete single-call mute for idempotent cleanup: only the named absence is suppressed and other exceptions escape.
Rust's standard library uses `Result` with `#[must_use]`; an intentional `let _ = ...` or `drop(...)` makes a best-effort discard explicit while `?` preserves propagation when the failure matters.
Go's standard library pairs `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` with filesystem operations so callers can mute only the documented 'already absent' case and propagate permission, I/O and other errors.
avoid_when: The failure carries information the caller needs, or the operation is not idempotent: send it through Result, Either or Option and make the caller decide.
The ignorability claim has not been demonstrated for the concrete failure value - a comment is not evidence; pin the documented contract or write the one test that establishes it.
The call sits on the main path of a request, booking, payment or migration: a muted failure there converts a repairable error into silent inconsistency - propagate it or record it as a failure.
The noise comes from an expected condition that recurs everywhere: model it instead (TryX API, status enum, Null Object, presence check) rather than muting it at each call site.
The failure is security-relevant - a permission check, integrity verification, quota or audit write: never mute it; fail closed and let the failure be observable (Fail-Safe Defaults).
anti_patterns: The blanket swallow: `catch (Exception ignore) {}`, `except Exception: pass`, a bare Ruby `rescue` modifier, or `_ =` on every error in a function - muting by omission, with no named failure type and no justification.

The whole-method mute wrapper: an entire body inside a helper that swallows Throwable (the jOOQ 'Mute-Design-Pattern' parody), so nobody - including the author - can tell which call inside was supposed to be ignorable.
Comment theatre: `// will never happen` on an empty catch with no evidence, copied forward until the code no longer contains the call that made it true.

Muting the diagnostic channel: ignoring logging, audit or metrics failures because 'telemetry must not fail the request', so the observability the incident needed disappears precisely when it matters.
Mute-as-fix: an ignore clause that suppresses a symptom (a race, a broken deployment, a missing migration) instead of the consequence of a provably harmless operation.
Test-side muting: `try: ... except: pass`, `let _ =` or an empty catch in fixture setup and teardown, so failures of the fixture disappear and the suite passes vacuously.
design_principles: Explicit over implicit: the intended ignore is written down (named failure type, explicit discard, documented suppression) so it is distinguishable from an accidental one at review time.
Narrow scope: mute the smallest call and the narrowest failure type; the construct must not be able to absorb failures that were never analysed.
Fail-safe by default for security-relevant failures: ignorance is defensible only for consequences that are provably harmless, never for checks that decide trust.
Locality of reasoning: the justification belongs at the call site where it can be re-checked, not in a global error handler that cannot see the call.
Single responsibility per mute: one reason per ignored failure; when a second reason appears, the mute is re-examined rather than extended.
best_practices: Name the narrowest swallowable failure type - one checked exception, one errno, one error class - and never Throwable, Exception, StandardError, a bare rescue, or a discard of a generic error value.

Write the reason next to the suppression as a checkable claim ('close on a read-only descriptor: the documented errors are EOF/EIO and neither can lose data here') rather than a shrug such as 'will never happen'.

Use the language's dedicated mute construct where one exists (Python contextlib.suppress, Swift try?, Ruby Kernel#suppress, optional catch binding, Go's named discard with a comment) - it states intent better than an empty handler.
Mark the discard explicitly for readers and analyzers: name the caught variable `ignored`, cast to void, attach `//nolint:errcheck` with the reason, so the site is greppable and reviewable.

Prefer the non-failing form of the operation when it exists (TryX API, non-throwing overload with an error_code out-parameter, presence check before the delete); the mute is for failures that must be tolerated, not for ones that can be avoided.
Keep a breadcrumb when the failure has any diagnostic value: a debug/trace-level log with context costs nothing at runtime and keeps the mute investigable.
Re-check the mute whenever the callee, its contract, the platform or the error policy changes; treat it as part of the review checklist for that call, not as a one-time decision.
sources: Java Design Patterns catalog (java-design-patterns.com), entry 'Mute Idiom' - also known as Exception Suppression / Quiet Exception; the catalog row this record materializes. Its Java example factors the mute into Mute.loggedMute(CheckedRunnable) and names the overuse hazard.
https://blog.jooq.org/the-mute-design-pattern/ - the parodic 'Mute-Design-Pattern' helper (catch (Throwable ignore), 'Will never happen hehe'); the demarcation this pattern must not cross.

https://cmu-sei.github.io/secure-coding-standards/sei-cert-c-coding-standard/recommendations/expressions-exp/exp12-c/ - CERT C EXP12-C: a deliberately unchecked return value must be cast explicitly 'to signify programmer intent'.

Bloch, J., Effective Java, 3rd ed. (2018) - the 'Don't ignore exceptions' item credited by the catalog entry: an ignored exception must be documented as expected, which is the discipline this idiom encodes.
